title: How a letter found a stranger in 5 handoffs
description:
In Stanley Milgram's small-world study, 296 people in Nebraska and Boston each got a folder for one Boston stockbroker, with one rule: you may only mail it to someone you know on a first-name basis. If each person knows 100 people, two hops reach 10,000 and five reach ten billion, but friends overlap, so what makes it work is the occasional friend who lives far away. 64 folders arrived, with 5.2 people in between on average, and 16 of them came through one clothing merchant in the stockbroker's hometown of Sharon. The study was published by Travers and Milgram in 1969.

Numbers checked in code: the paper's counts, 100 to the power of each hop, the Omaha-Boston distance (about 1,280 miles), and a 100,000-person network model where 1 far friend in 100 cuts the average handoffs from about 5,000 to about 19. Source: Travers & Milgram, Sociometry 32(4), 1969; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_experiment

social_caption: A letter from Nebraska reached a stranger in Boston in about 5 handoffs between friends. Here's the math of why the world is so small.
facts_checked: Travers & Milgram 1969 (Sociometry 32(4)): 296 starting volunteers, 196 in Nebraska and 100 in Boston; the target was a Boston stockbroker who lived in Sharon, Mass.; the document could be sent only to a first-name acquaintance, chosen to advance it toward the target (https://www.cse.cuhk.edu.hk/~cslui/CMSC5734/travers69smallworld.pdf)
64 folders reached the target; mean number of intermediaries in completed chains 5.2; 16 of the 64 came through one clothing merchant in Sharon (25%) (same paper)
Milgram's experiments began in 1967 at Harvard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small-world_experiment)
Omaha to Boston great-circle distance 2,058 km = 1,279 miles, said as 1,300 (verify.py)
Model: 100,000 people on a ring, each knowing 10 neighbours: 5,000 handoffs on average; with 1% of friendships rewired to random far-away people: 18.6 (verify.py, BFS)

beats.say: A letter from Nebraska found a stranger in Boston in 5 handoffs.
No address. Each person could only mail it to someone they knew by first name.
Stanley Milgram sent out 296 folders, all for one Boston stockbroker.
You're in Omaha, holding one. Don't guess. Mail it to the friend most likely to know him: someone in Boston, or in stocks.
Why that works: you know about 100 people. They know 100 each. Two hops: 10,000. Five hops: ten billion.
beats.caption: Why that works: you know about 100 people. They know 100 each. Two hops: 10,000. Five hops: 10,000,000,000.

beats.say: But your friends all know each other. That overlap should kill it.
It doesn't, because of the friend who moved away. One cousin in Boston jumps 1,300 miles in a single hop.
64 folders made it, with 5.2 people in between. One in four came through a single shop owner in his hometown.
So who would you mail it to first?
